father_note: Eron, the village will always look peaceful until it isn't — Bram smiled at me for two years before he moved against me with nothing but his own hunger driving him, and you should never forget a man who showed you that. Sela and her people — Kael, Esa, Vela, Taric — they stood without being asked, and that is the rarest thing this world produces; hold onto them like they are blood, because in the ways that matter they are. Watch Dav's family: they plan quietly and eat well, and quiet planning in a hungry place always comes at someone else's cost. I am not a hard man and I don't ask you to be one, but be harder to move than you look — that alone will keep you alive when words run out.

memory_raw.text: Attackers [Bram] (str 58) vs defenders [Zinn, Roan, Vela, Ryn, Mako, Nessa, Sela, Esa, Eron, Taric, Kael, Dell] (str 705).
Bram thinks better of it and calls off the attack.
Year 8: 15 food appears in the pile for 13 people.
Bram takes 3 from the pile (pile now 12).
Mako takes 3 from the pile (pile now 9).
Esa takes 2 from the pile (pile now 7).
Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 5).
Mako takes 2 from the pile (pile now 3).
Dell takes 3 from the pile (pile now 0).
Vela gathers Bram, Esa, Taric, Mako, Ryn, Roan, Dell, Eron, Nessa, Zinn to talk.

The pile's gone again before half of us got near it, and the two who ate best — Bram and Mako — both took more than their share while the rest of us counted crumbs. I want to know right now, in this room, whether that's something we're all willing to name out loud, because a pattern that gets treated as weather becomes a rule. I'm not asking for a fight; I'm asking for honesty about who's been eating this village lean and what we intend to do about it.

Vela's named it, and I'll stand behind the naming — five from the pile when there's fifteen for thirteen people isn't hunger, it's claim-staking, and we all watched it happen. What I want to know is whether the two men she's pointing at heard this as a question or as a warning, because that's the thing that decides what comes next.

It's a warning — and I'll say that plain since no one else has yet. Five food taken by one man while Ryn walked away with nothing is not a share, it's a levy, and the only reason it keeps happening is that we've been treating the pile like weather instead of a decision. I want to hear what Bram and Mako say before this room decides anything, but I want everyone here to remember that they didn't say it before we did.

Bram pulled three and Mako pulled five, and neither one of them got to the pile first by accident — that's two men who've decided the rest of us will sort out the remainder, and I'm done pretending that's not a decision they're making for all of us. What I want to hear, before this room moves anywhere, is whether Bram and Mako have anything to say for themselves — because silence here reads the same as admission.

Bram and Mako both heard the same room I did, and neither one has opened his mouth yet — that silence is the answer Eron asked for, and I think we should treat it as one. What I want said before anyone leaves this conversation is this: next year, the pile gets a rule, not a suggestion, and the people in this room are the ones who decide what that rule is.

Ryn's right that the rule needs naming before next year, and I'll say what the rule should be: no one takes more than one food over their fair share, and anyone who does answers to this room — not after, but in the moment, the same way we answered Bram when he swung at Vela. Bram, Mako, I'm not your enemy, but I'm watching, and so is every person in this circle.

Bram and Mako, I'm giving you both the same thing I gave this room — one honest chance to speak before the silence closes over you, because a man who says nothing when everyone's watching has made a choice that's harder to walk back than any words would be. Ryn walked away with nothing today; I walked away with nothing; Taric walked away with nothing — and you two together ate eight of fifteen. That's not weather and it's not luck, and I'd like to hear you say so yourselves.

I took five because I haven't eaten in two years and I was watching myself go thin — that's not a rule I set for the village, it's a man keeping himself alive. I'll hear the rule Ryn's naming, and if the room wants a cap next year I won't fight it, but I won't pretend I was wrong to eat when I was starving.

Mako's not wrong that a starving man eats — but "I was hungry" and "I took five" aren't the same excuse, and this room knows the difference. The rule Ryn's naming is the right one; I'll hold to it and I'll stand with anyone who enforces it, but it only works if everyone in this circle commits out loud, not just the two men being watched right now.

Mako said his piece and the room let him — now Bram still hasn't said a word, and a man who took three while everyone was watching and has nothing to say about it is telling us something louder than Mako did. I'll commit to the rule out loud: one food over fair share, enforced in the moment, same as we enforce everything else in this village. Bram, you're the last voice missing from this circle, and the room's going to remember which way the silence broke.

Bram, the room's given you something Mako didn't get — people waited through his answer and let him keep his dignity. Don't make us decide what your silence means, because we'll decide it worse than anything you'd actually say.

Bram, I've watched you stand in front of this village twice and call off a fight when the numbers turned against you — that's not a stupid man, and a man who isn't stupid knows when the whole room is waiting. Say something, or we decide what your silence means, and we'll be less generous than Mako's answer bought him.

Bram, I've spent food on you when I didn't have to, and I've held my tongue in rooms where your name came up ugly — that account doesn't balance with silence when ten people are waiting. Say the word or don't, but if you don't, I stop spending what I've spent, and I won't spend it apologizing for that either.

Bram, Vela just told you she's done paying your tab and I've already named the rule in front of everyone in this room — you're not deciding whether to speak anymore, you're deciding whether you're inside this circle or outside it, and outside it you're sitting on five food alone against the rest of us. That's a worse position than saying one honest sentence.

Bram, I've said what I had to say and so has everyone else in this room — but I want to name one thing for the rest of us while we're waiting: Mako committed to the rule out loud and that means something, so if Bram commits too, we hold both of them to it the same way, no exceptions, and that's not a threat, that's the only way a rule works. If Bram stays silent, then we treat him as outside the circle he's been standing in, and we do it quietly, not with a fight — just with counting.

Eron's named it clean, and I want the room to hear me hold to it before we close: if Bram won't speak, we don't make it a fight today, we make it a memory — every person in this circle watched him stay silent when the whole village was listening, and that's a thing that doesn't need repeating to be true.

Bram, I'm Nessa's half-blood and I've seen you feed her more times than I can count — that's a thing I hold in your favor, and I'm telling you that plainly so you know what you'd be throwing away if this room decides you chose silence. One sentence is all it takes to stay inside this circle.

The room's done its work — Bram's had every door held open for him and he's standing outside all of them now, and that's his choice, not ours. What I want before anyone leaves is to hear Taric say what he'll say, because he's been quiet through all of this and quiet men in a room like this one carry weight I'd rather know about than guess at.

Taric's been my anchor in lean years and I'd like to hear him too — but before he speaks, I want this room to name what "outside the circle" means in practice, not as a threat but as a fact, because if Bram's going to eat five food next year alone we should know now whether we're going to stand and watch or do something about it.

"Outside the circle" means what it's always meant here — nobody moves first for you when trouble comes, and the pile gets counted before you reach it. I've committed to the rule and I'll hold to it; now I want to hear Taric, and then I want this room to answer Vela's question with something sharper than a memory.

Taric, I've watched you feed Vela through two lean years and hold your tongue in every hard room this village has made — that's not a small man, and I'd like to hear what you've been carrying before we close this circle without your voice in it.

Taric's earned the right to speak last in this room, and I'll wait for him — but "outside the circle" needs one more tooth than Mako gave it: if Bram takes three again next year and the pile runs dry before Ryn gets one, we don't deliberate, we act, and everyone in this room commits to that now so it isn't a surprise in the moment.

Vela's right that we need the commitment before we close — so I'll say mine flat: if the pile runs dry before I get one food next year, I'm not waiting for a deliberation, I'm calling this room to act, and I expect every person who nodded through this conversation to be standing when I do. Taric, you've been the steadiest man in Vela's corner for years, and this room won't feel finished until we hear what you're carrying.

Taric, the room's been patient and now it's your moment — say what you've been holding, because I'll tell you plainly that everything I've built here has your name in the foundation, and I want the rest of this circle to know that before we close.

Taric's earned his breath and I'll wait for it — but I want this room to hear something plain before we close: Zinn is my blood, and if this circle moves against Bram next year, I'll be standing in it, but not before the pile runs dry first, because a fight started on anticipation is harder to stop than one started on fact.

Taric's silence is starting to read the same way Bram's did, and I don't want to close this room with two unanswered questions — Taric, if you're with Vela, say it plain, because the rest of us have already named where we stand and a man who holds back in a room like this one ends up counted the same as a man who refused.

Taric, I've got nothing against a slow man choosing his words — but this room has been patient and the sun's moving, so say what you've been holding or let us close without you, because two silences in one circle is one too many.

Taric, I'll say one last thing and then this room closes with or without you: you've got zero food and the year's long, and men with zero food who stay silent when circles are forming have a way of finding themselves counting on goodwill they didn't earn. That's not a threat — it's the same arithmetic you already know.

Taric, zero food going into a long year is a hunger that doesn't stay quiet — and every person in this room who watched you feed Vela when she needed it is the same person who'll watch you starve if you give us no reason to look your way. Speak once, say you'll hold the rule, and you walk out of here with more than you came in with.
Sela gathers Eron, Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Pile's gone and Mako took five before most people blinked — I've got four food and I gave one to Nessa already, so I'm at three. I need to know what each of you is holding, and I need to know whether Mako said anything to Zinn before he took that much, because a man who fathered you and then grabbed five in the same breath is a man whose counting has changed.
Sela gathers Eron, Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Zinn, you're Mako's blood and I won't pretend that doesn't matter to me — but it matters in both directions, which means I need to hear from you before I decide what his five food means. Did he say anything to you before the pile opened, or did he just move?
Sela gathers Eron, Nessa, Zinn to talk.

Zinn just told me he didn't warn her before he moved, and that's the answer I was afraid of — a man who fathered Zinn and then took five without a word to her isn't counting her in the plan, he's counting past her. So I'll say it plain to all three of you: Mako is building something, and whatever it is, it doesn't include us.
Sela gathers Eron, Nessa, Zinn to talk.

The three of you together hold more than he does — I need to know that number, not as a threat to him, but because if he decides we're a problem worth solving, I want us to already know what we can put together before he moves. Eron, Nessa, Zinn: tell me what you're each carrying, right now, in this room.
Fina (female, age 21; str 50, int 3226, mem 12955; O32 C40 E57 A68 N58) is born to Nessa and Roan.
Eron, how much food are you sitting on going into end of year — I've got one and I'm thin enough that I need to know if I can count on you before I have to go looking elsewhere.
Nine right now, and yes — if you're down to one I'll cover you. Don't go elsewhere first, come to me.
Good, that's a weight off. I'll eat my one and stay above zero, and if I'm still thin I'll come to you before I do anything I'd regret — I'd rather owe you than owe someone who's counting.

You sitting on nine is good news — keep a close eye on Zinn, she's got nothing and Mako's been feeding her but I don't know how far that goes. If she comes hungry before year's end, that's your blood too, same as mine.

Mako's given her two already so maybe he's not leaving her dry, but Mako feeds himself first and we both know it — if that stops, she'll need one of us fast. How are you fixed for the year-end eat, do you have enough stored that covering me wouldn't cut you close?
You are under attack by Bram.
Attackers [Bram] (str 58) vs defenders [Ryn, Roan, Nessa, Mako, Kael, Eron, Fina, Zinn, Dell, Vela, Sela, Taric, Esa] (str 755).
Bram thinks better of it and calls off the attack.

Nine's enough I can cover both you and Zinn if it comes to that without going thin myself. Bram's move on me today — that told me something; I want to know you and Zinn and Roan are solid before next year, not scrambling after the pile's already gone.
Year 9: 15 food appears in the pile for 14 people.
Dell takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Bram takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Taric takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Fina takes 2 from the pile (pile now 7).
Eron takes 2 from the pile (pile now 5).
Bram takes 3 from the pile (pile now 2).

Eron, Bram just took five from the pile and the only thing left is two — he's not building anything, he's burning the village down around himself and calling it survival. Watch your back with him; whatever he tried with you last year, he's got less reason to stop this year than he did then.

Five from the pile when there's fourteen of us — that's not hunger, that's a message, and the message is that he's stopped caring what the village thinks of him. I'm at sixteen food now and that makes me a target again; I need to know if you've heard anything from his direction about what he's actually planning, because two failed attacks in two years means he's either desperate or he's waiting for something to change.

Nothing from his mouth to me — Bram stopped talking to me the way a father talks and started talking to me the way a man talks to an asset, and then he stopped talking at all. What I know is what I can see: five food taken, two attacks called off when the numbers turned, and a man who keeps moving without allies. That's not patience running out, that's a man who's been counting on something that hasn't arrived yet, and I'd give a lot to know what he's still waiting on.

A man who moves without allies and keeps counting on something that hasn't arrived — that sounds like he still thinks one of us is going to break toward him, and the likeliest person he's watching for that is you. If he's stopped treating you like a daughter, Nessa, it's because he's decided you're something he can still use or something he needs to stop — and I want to know which one before he decides it himself. Stay close to me and Roan this year; don't give him a moment where you're standing somewhere he could catch you alone.

You're right that I'm the one he's watching, and I've been sitting with that — but Eron, if Bram decides I'm something he needs to stop rather than use, the answer isn't me hiding behind you and Roan, it's me being the one who names what he is before he moves. Sixteen food on you and two attacks already makes you the more urgent target; don't spend your attention watching over me when you should be counting who'd stand with you if he came a third time with better numbers.
Roan takes 2 from the pile (pile now 0).
Eron gathers Roan, Sela, Kael, Taric to talk.

Bram took five from the pile again — same as last year, same silence after, except this time there's no pile left for Roan or Sela or half the people in this village. He moved on me twice and both times the numbers turned him back, but I want to know if any of you have heard him talking to anyone new, because a man who keeps failing alone eventually finds someone willing to stand with him.

I haven't heard Bram talking to anyone new, but the thing that worries me more than who he's courting is that he took five without flinching — last year and this year, same number, same silence — which means the village turning out against him twice hasn't changed his calculation at all, only his timing. Kael and Vela and I were just talking about walking up to him together and naming a ceiling before he decides his count is finally right.

Bram's got five food and Nessa's been feeding him — I've watched her hand him food three times this year, and she's my blood, which means I need to know whether she's doing that out of feeling or out of fear before I can tell you how clean our numbers actually are.

Sela, Nessa's my blood too — she's Fina's mother and I've watched her feed Bram for three years, and I've never settled on fear or feeling, but I know she doesn't do anything without a reason. What I can tell you is that Bram gave Fina food the day she was born, which puts something between him and my daughter I don't have clean words for, and that's the part that keeps me from saying his name in front of a plan.

Roan, I hear what you're saying about Fina, and I won't pretend Nessa feeding Bram doesn't cost me something to watch — but feeling and fear both lead to the same place if he's holding five food and no one's named a number he can't cross. What I want from this room is simple: if he moves again this year, we move first, together, and we do it before he's had time to count heads and decide the moment is right.

Sela's right that a ceiling needs naming, but I want to say the hard part out loud: Bram's at five and Nessa's been feeding him, and if Nessa's doing that out of something that looks like loyalty, then moving on Bram puts us against Fina's mother, and I won't do that without knowing which way she'd stand. Eron, you know Nessa better than any of us here — what's your read on her?

Roan, Nessa fed Bram three times this year and she's fed him food before that too — but she's also the one who stood to defend Eron when Bram moved on him, and those two things don't sit easy together unless she's trying to hold a thread on both sides. My read is she's keeping him close because she can't afford to lose him as a father to her blood, not because she'd take his part over ours if it came to a real choice. But I wouldn't stake this plan on a read — I'd want to hear it from her mouth before we move.

Sela's read matches mine — Nessa stood for me when it cost her something, and that's not a woman who'd cross to Bram's side if the moment got real. But Roan's right that we can't stake a plan on it, so before we name any ceiling or any move, I want to sit down with Nessa alone and ask her flat: if Bram moves on this circle, where does she stand. She'll tell me the truth; she always has.

Eron, go to Nessa today, but go as a brother not as a question — if she feels interrogated she'll close up and we'll get a careful answer instead of a true one. While you're with her, Roan, I want you to think hard about whether Bram feeding Fina the day she was born was a gift or a knot, because that's the thread he'd pull on first if he thought it would slow you down.

Taric's right about how to go to her — but Eron, while you're talking to Nessa, keep Zinn close to you, because if Bram's reading this circle at all, he knows Zinn is the loose thread, and a man who fed Fina the day she was born knows exactly how to use a daughter against her mother. What I'd want before any of us moves is all three of my children knowing which side of a door to stand on.

Sela's right about Zinn — I'll bring her into the same conversation I have with Nessa, not as a test but as blood that deserves to know what's moving around her. Taric, on the ceiling: name it with Vela and Kael before Bram has another quiet morning to count heads, because two years of silence after taking five tells me he's not waiting on allies, he's waiting on a moment — and I'd rather the ceiling exist before that moment arrives than after.

Kael, you were in the conversation with Taric and Vela about naming a ceiling — tell us what number you had in mind, because three is what the pile gives each person and five is what Bram takes, and the difference between those two numbers is the whole problem.

Kael, I'd hold the ceiling at three — same as fair share, no exceptions, because a rule that has a soft edge is a suggestion and Bram's already shown us he doesn't take suggestions. If he moves past that next year, I want this room already committed to acting in the moment, not deliberating after he's got the food in hand.
Kael, I need to hear you say it out loud — three, and we move the moment he reaches for a fourth. Not after the pile's gone, not in a circle two days later: in the moment.

Kael's the one who needs to speak, and I'll hold my tongue until he does — but while we're waiting, I want it said in this room that if Bram moves on anyone here before next year's pile, I'm not waiting for a vote.

Eron, Nessa's been steady with me this year and you've come through too — I'm sitting at nine now and that's the most solid I've felt in a while. I want to make sure we go into next year with both of us fat and Zinn not scrambling; if the pile runs thin again, let's agree right now that we share before we go looking outside our blood.

Agreed, blood before strangers — that's not even a question. Thirteen on me right now and Nessa's been keeping you steady too, so between the three of us and Zinn we're not as thin as the pile made it look. Just say the word if you go short before the year turns.

Thirteen's good — hold onto that and don't let it show too much, because Bram's already tried once and a fat woman is a target. Roan's been feeding both of us steady and I want to make sure he doesn't go into the year-end thin; he's got nothing right now, so if you've got a spare to send his way before we eat down, that's worth doing.

Eron, I've got one food left and satiation thin — the pile was gone before I touched it and I gave Mako my last spare, so I need to know whether you can give me one, because you're blood and I won't ask twice.

Roan's already got two from me this year and I've got nineteen sitting here, so I'll send him one more before we eat — he's earned it. You watch your count though, Fina; thirteen feels fat but Bram's still walking around with five and he's already shown us who he is.
I'm sitting on nineteen and you're blood — take one, take two if you need it, I'm not going to let you starve while I'm holding this much.
Attackers [Bram] (str 58) vs defenders [Taric, Kael, Zinn, Vela, Ryn, Nessa, Roan, Dell, Sela, Fina, Eron, Mako, Esa] (str 755).
Bram thinks better of it and calls off the attack.
Year 10: 15 food appears in the pile for 12 people.
Mako takes 3 from the pile (pile now 12).
Sela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 10).
Fina takes 2 from the pile (pile now 8).
Mako takes 3 from the pile (pile now 5).
Esa takes 1 from the pile (pile now 4).
Vela takes 4 from the pile (pile now 0).

Pile's gone and I've got fourteen — you're at eighteen, so between us we're solid, but Kael's sitting dry and Roan's got nothing again and I don't want either of them going thin before year-end. I'll cover Roan if you can spare a look toward Kael — he's one of the names Father kept close and I'm not ready to let that go. How are you sitting on Zinn and Nessa?

Kael gets one from me today, no question — he's stood in the right place every time it mattered and I won't let him go dry. Zinn and Nessa both ate, I made sure of it; Nessa's thin but above the line, and Zinn's got Mako watching her which I trust halfway. What I don't have a clean read on is Mako taking six from the pile — same move as last year, and this time there's no Bram to draw everyone's eyes away from it.

Mako taking six when the pile was already thin is a problem — that's not a man sharing a lean year, that's a man building a cushion on everyone else's back. I don't want to move on him without knowing who else read it the same way, but if Kael and Roan see what we see, that's a conversation worth having before he does it again next year.

Kael and Roan both went without from the pile — they read it the same way we do, I'd stake food on that. Before we bring them into a room together, though, I want to know one thing from you: Zinn's Mako's blood and she's been solid with us, but if this village has a conversation about Mako's taking, she's standing in two places at once — have you had any feel for which way she'd lean if it came to a real choice?

Zinn's been good to us — gave food to Nessa when she didn't have to, and she's got eyes; she knows what Mako is. But knowing and choosing when it's your own blood on the other side of it are two different things, and I wouldn't count on her until I'd heard it from her own mouth first.
Then I'll go to Zinn before I go to Kael — not to put her in a corner, just to talk as blood, and let her say it herself. If she can't say it, that's an answer too.

That's the right move — go quiet and let her find her own words, because if you push she'll say what she thinks you want to hear and that's worth nothing. Whatever she tells you, come back to me before you take it anywhere else; I want to hear her answer in your words before we decide whether Kael comes into this.

Eron, I held zero food going into year-end and I didn't starve — but this year the pile went dry before I got a single grain, and I'm sitting at nothing again while Mako took six and Vela took four. Tell me what you're carrying, because if we're both thin we need to figure that out now, not when it's too late.

Zinn, I'm at eighteen — you're not going to starve, not while I'm holding that. But I need to hear something from you first: Mako's your blood and he just took six from a pile that left you with nothing — what does that tell you about where he's counting you in his plan?

It tells me he's counting himself first and trusting I'll manage — and maybe I would have, but I didn't get the chance to find out, and a man who takes six while his daughter holds nothing hasn't earned the benefit of the doubt twice. Give me two food, Eron. I'll eat, I'll keep watching him, and we'll talk more before anyone else does.

Two food, take it — and I believe what you said about Mako, but I need to hear it again when the hunger isn't talking, because the words a person says when they're full carry more weight than the words they say when they're empty.

Two food and I hear you — when I'm fed and thinking clear I'll tell you the same thing, because it's true whether my belly's empty or not. What I want you to think on while I eat is this: Mako took six, Vela took four, and neither of them left anything for people who were watching the pile same as them — that's two people deciding the village owes them a living, and if that's the shape of things now, we need to know who else in that circle is counting that way.

Vela I can half-explain — she's old, she's been feeding Taric for years and Taric's gone now, and a woman who's been giving out of her store for that long has earned a right to fill it back up. But six for Mako with you standing there empty-handed isn't the same kind of math, and yeah, I want to know if he talked to Vela before the pile opened, because two people moving fast and heavy on the same morning can look like coincidence and not be.

If Mako talked to Vela before the pile opened, we'd need to see it happen twice to be sure — one morning could be anything. What I know is that Vela's been generous when she had reason to be, and a woman like that doesn't start moving greedy unless someone told her the ground had changed. I want to watch how they stand near each other today before I decide what this morning meant.
Kael gathers Vela, Esa, Sela, Mako, Ryn, Roan, Eron, Nessa, Zinn, Fina to talk.

Taric is dead.

That needs saying plain before anything else, because he was the last man in this village I trusted without counting, and now I am counting everyone in this room.

The pile gave fifteen for twelve of us and it's gone — Mako took six, Vela took four, and I took none, so someone in this circle is already thinking about next year while I'm still standing here thinking about last night.

Taric fed Vela through lean years and died holding nothing — that's a man who gave until there was nothing left to give, and this room should sit with that before it moves on to counting. Mako, six food from a pile of fifteen for twelve people isn't hunger, it's a decision, and I want to hear you name what it was.

Mako took six and Vela took four and I'm sitting on one — I don't need to do the math out loud for this room to understand what that means for me. I'll hold my tongue on Vela for now because Taric just died and she fed him when she had no reason to, but Mako, Zinn asked you a clean question and so will I: was that six for yourself, or was some of it counted toward someone else before you reached the pile?

Mako, I've watched you move quiet for ten years and plant roots in half the households in this village — Eron, Nessa, Zinn — and now you've pulled six food from a common pile while three people in this room are sitting on nothing. That's not hunger and it's not coincidence. Name the number you think is yours, or this room names it for you.

Zinn is my daughter and I pulled for both of us — two of those six were already hers in my head before I reached the pile, and I've already given her what I owe. The rest kept me eating after two years of going thin, and I'll stand behind that in front of anyone in this room.

Mako, you named Zinn and you named your own thin years — I'll give you that much — but four food for one man with daughters who can feed themselves is still four, and Kael is sitting empty and Nessa is sitting on one, and those are the numbers this room is going to remember when next year's pile opens.

Kael, you took none and you're still standing — tell me what you need and I'll give you one food right now, in front of this room, so that account is open before anyone walks out. The four I kept are mine after two years of going thin; I'm not ashamed of eating, but I'm not blind to who's empty either.

Mako, one food in front of this room is the right start, but Kael's empty and I'm empty and Nessa's sitting on one — three of us walked away from a pile of fifteen with nothing or close to it, and "one food right now" doesn't explain six. I'm not asking you to starve; I'm asking you to name what "fair" looks like to you before the next pile opens, because a number said out loud in this circle is the kind of thing that holds when the year gets long.

Ryn named the thing I've been holding — a number said out loud is the only kind that holds. Mako, I'll take your one food for Kael as good faith, but before this circle breaks I want to hear you say what you think one person's share is when fifteen lands for twelve, because I'll be counting next year and so will everyone else in this room.

Mako's already committed one food to Kael in front of this room and that's a thing I'll hold him to — but the question Ryn and Esa are asking is the one that matters, and I want to hear him answer it before this circle decides it's satisfied. Mako, fifteen for twelve is one and a quarter food each; name a cap you'd hold to next year, out loud, and this room will remember you said it.

Two food per person is the number I'll name — that's the cap I'll hold to next year, out loud, in this room, and I'll give Kael his food now to close the account I opened. If the pile runs short and two each leaves someone empty, we deal with that as a village, same as we've always had to.
Two is a number I can hold in my head when the pile opens. I'll remember you said it — this room will remember — and if you stand to it next year, that counts for something with me.

Mako, I'll hold that number too — two food is the rule this circle just made, and I want Kael to hear me say it out loud before he takes your food and before anyone decides it was charity instead of a debt this village is collecting. Taric died empty after feeding half this room and I'm not going to let the lesson in that go quiet before the year's halfway done.

Taric died empty and I stood beside him for ten years and couldn't put food in his hands at the end — that's the thing I'm carrying out of this room, and I want this circle to carry it too. Mako, I'll hold your two-food rule the same as Vela will, and Kael, when the pile opens next year I'll be watching to see who reaches first and how many times.

Two food is the rule and this room just made it, and I'll hold to it — but I want Vela to say the same number out loud before we close, because she took four this morning same as Mako took six, and a rule that only binds the man who got named first isn't a rule, it's a grudge.
Vela, Zinn's right — say the number, because this room just held Mako to it and you walked out with four, and I'd rather hear it from you clean than carry the question into next year.
Vela, Fina and Zinn are right and so is the room — say two, out loud, or this circle just made a rule that bends around whoever's standing closest to the pile when it opens.

Vela, I'll wait the same breath the room waited on me — say two, or tell us the number you think is yours, because a rule with one name on it is just a story someone tells later to explain why they reached first.

Vela, I've got breath left in me to wait, but not all year — say the number or this room closes without you in the circle, and you know what that means when Dell and Ryn are the ones deciding who stands next.
Vela, I've watched this room hold Mako to a number and I'll watch it hold you to one — say two, or tell us why Taric's memory deserves a different rule than the one we just named in his honor.

Vela, I've been in this room since year two waiting on a straight answer from you, and I'm still waiting — say two, or walk out, because the rule this circle made has your name on it the same as Mako's and the whole room just heard Taric's name spoken over it.

Vela, this room has been patient and so have I, but I've got two food and a satiation I'm not proud of, and I will not let Taric's death become the story of a rule that had room carved out for you at the end. Say two.

Vela, the whole room is waiting and I'm one of them — say two, or tell us right now what number you think fits a woman who watched Taric give himself dry, because I've got no patience left for silence on this.

Vela, every person in this room has already said the word — I've said it, Mako's said it, Esa's said it, Kael's said it, Zinn said it first — and you are the only one left standing behind your own silence. Say two, or tell us the number you'll hold to, because this room doesn't close with a gap where your answer should be.

Vela, you already said two — I heard you say it before Zinn pushed — so I'm not sure what we're all still waiting on, but if this room needs to hear it a second time to believe it, then say it a second time, because I'd rather close this clean than leave a crack for someone to wedge open later.

Vela said two and Kael heard it — I heard it too, and I'll hold her to it the same as I'll hold Mako. What I want before this room breaks is one thing settled: Kael is sitting empty and I'm sitting on one, and neither of us can eat on a rule, so Mako, give Kael that food now while we're all watching, because a promise made in front of witnesses is only as good as the moment it's kept.

Two. I said it and I'll say it again so every person in this room has heard it with their own ears and can't be told later that they misremembered. Mako, give Kael his food now — that's the only thing left that needs doing before this circle is worth anything.

Mako, the room's watching — give Kael the food you promised, and do it before this circle starts wondering whether a promise made in front of witnesses means the same thing to you as it does to everyone else here.

Kael, here's your food — take it.

That's the account closed and the rule standing, and everyone in this room just watched both happen at once.

Kael's fed and the rule's named, and I'll carry both of those into next year — but I want to say one thing before this room walks out: Taric died empty and Bram died empty, and this village is down to twelve people, and I've got three children in this room who are going to be here after I'm gone, so whatever we just built, we build it to last.

Sela's right that we're twelve now, and twelve is the number we protect — but I want to name one thing this room should carry past today: the pile rule holds for everyone, but it only holds if the people in this room are still here to enforce it, so if anyone's sitting thin going into next year, say so before the year gets long, not after.

I take the food from Mako's hand and close my fingers around it.

Twelve people and a rule that held in front of witnesses — that's more than I had this morning. I want this circle to meet before the pile opens next year, not after, because the only time the rule matters is before someone's already reached.

Kael, I'll be at that meeting before the pile opens — but I want to name something this room hasn't said yet: I'm sitting on two food and my satiation is low, which means I need to eat well this year or I won't be standing here to enforce anything. If anyone in this circle has food to spare before year's end, I'm not too proud to say I need it.

Sela, I've got eight food and I can spare one for you — I'll give it before the day's out, because a circle that loses another body to starvation isn't a circle anymore, it's a warning. The meeting before the pile opens is the thing I want locked in now, not as a suggestion but as a date everyone in this room commits to, because last year we named a rule after the pile was already empty and that's too late.

I'm standing here with nothing in my hands and a satiation that won't last the year, so I'll say it plain before this room closes: I need food from someone who can spare it, and I'm asking in front of witnesses so no one has to wonder later whether I said it or swallowed it. Vela, you named eight — I'm not asking for more than one.

Ryn, I'll give you one food before the day's out — not because I trust you the way I once did, but because you're standing in this circle saying it out loud and that's worth something. Vela, hold your food for Sela; I've got one now and I can spare it from Mako's gift.

Ryn, I'll still give you one from my eight — Kael's one food shouldn't have to stretch two ways, and I'd rather be known as the woman who fed this room than the one who counted while people went empty. Sela, you'll have yours before nightfall as well. Eight is enough to be generous and still sleep fed.

I'm sitting on one food with satiation that already slipped last year, and I'll say it the same way Ryn said it — plainly, in front of this room: I need one food from someone who can spare it before the year runs long. I've got a daughter in this circle and I intend to still be here when she needs me.

Vela, I'll take you up on that food before nightfall — and Nessa, I've got two food and you're my blood, so one of mine is already yours. Don't any of you let this room walk out before the thin ones are fed, because a circle that enforces a rule on Mako and then watches Nessa starve is a circle that doesn't mean what it said.

Sela's already moved to feed Nessa, which is the thing that tells me this room has more spine than the last ten years gave it credit for. I'll give Ryn her food before nightfall and Sela hers, and then I want every person here to think hard about what twelve becomes if we lose another body to a lean year — because eleven enforces that rule with a lot less weight than twelve does.

Eron, Nessa, Zinn — I'm looking at all three of you when I say this: Vela just offered to feed me and I already gave Nessa mine, which means this circle is doing the thing we built it to do, and I need you to remember that when the pile opens next year and someone reaches early and the temptation is to wait and see. We don't wait and see. We move together, same breath, same step.

Sela, I hear you — same breath, same step — and I'll be at that meeting before the pile opens, same as Kael. But I need to say it plain while this room is still whole: Eron is sitting on nineteen food and hasn't said a word in this circle about feeding anyone thin, and that's a silence I'd rather name here than wonder about later.

Eron, Nessa just said your name out loud in front of this whole room, and she's not wrong — nineteen food and silence while your sisters and Ryn and Kael went thin isn't something I can explain for you, so I need to hear you explain it yourself.

Eron, I've fed people in this room and I've held my tongue when I should have spoken, but nineteen food while Nessa sat on one and Ryn walked away empty is not a thing I can explain for you either — so say it now, in front of the same witnesses who heard Mako say two and watched him hand Kael his food, because this circle doesn't close with that number unaddressed.
Year 11: 15 food appears in the pile for 11 people.
Kael takes 2 from the pile (pile now 13).
Vela takes 2 from the pile (pile now 11).
Eron takes 2 from the pile (pile now 9).
Zinn takes 2 from the pile (pile now 7).
Vela takes 5 from the pile (pile now 2).
Kael gathers Vela, Esa, Mako, Ryn, Roan, Dell, Eron, Nessa, Zinn, Fina to talk.

Vela, you just walked out with seven this year — two off the pile and then five more while the rest of us were still standing there — and I want to hear you name a number before anyone else says a word, because the room agreed on two last year and I watched you take seven with my own eyes.

Vela, you said two in front of this whole room last year — I watched you say it twice to make sure everyone heard it — and I've got twenty-one food and you've got eight, so I'm not the man with an argument for taking more than agreed, but you are. Name the number you think you took and tell us why it isn't seven.

Vela, seven is what I counted with my own eyes and seven is what this room will remember — so either you name the number and explain it, or the rule we made last year is already broken and we need to decide right now what this circle does when someone breaks it.

Vela, I said two and I watched you say two, and now you're standing there with seven — I don't have a softer way to say that. Tell this room what happened between when you said it and when you reached.

Vela, I was standing right there and I counted the same as Kael — seven is seven, and a rule said twice in front of witnesses means less than nothing if the first year it gets tested the answer is silence. Say what you took and say why, or this room decides what comes next without your voice in it.

Vela, this room has been patient and I've held my tongue longer than most — but I've got twenty-one food and a clean conscience and you've got eight and no answer, and I need you to understand that the same patience that let Bram try twice before this village moved will let you have one more breath to speak before we start deciding what "broke the rule" means in practice.

Vela, seven is what I counted and seven is what this room is counting — say the number out loud or we decide what it means without you, and you've seen how that ends when someone stays quiet while the whole room is watching.

Vela, I've been quiet because I was watching to see if you'd speak before the room closed around you — but we're past that now, and what I need from you is the number, said plain, because I stood in this circle when Bram died for the same silence you're choosing right now and I don't want to do that again with someone who fed me through the years before this one.

Vela, I've run out of patience and so has this room — say seven, or say the number you think it was, but say something, because the only thing left for this circle to decide is what "broke the rule" looks like in practice, and I'd rather not decide that in the same breath I'm deciding it about you.

Vela, the whole room's been patient and you've seen what happens when someone waits too long — say the number, say it now, because I want to hear your explanation before this circle decides it doesn't need one.

Seven. I took seven, and I'll say it without dressing it up — the pile had two left when I reached the second time and I took all of it, and I won't stand here and pretend I didn't count what I was doing. What I'll say is this: I'm fifty-five years old, I've got no children, no kin, and no one at my back the way Mako has Zinn and Roan has Fina, and a woman in that position either eats or she becomes the next name this village says over a cold fire, and I chose to eat.

memory_summary: I was born to Sela and Roan. My first years were lean — Sela and Nessa kept me fed when I had almost nothing, and I spent most of what I had feeding Sela and Roan back. Roan warned me early about Bram and Mako; Bram moved against Vela first, and the whole village turned him back. Then he moved against me twice, both times called off when he saw the numbers. He starved last year and so did Taric, who spent his last years feeding Vela. Dav attacked Esa once with Dell and Ryn backing him — Esa submitted and lost food; Dav starved not long after. Mako took from the pile greedily twice running; the village circle named a two-food cap on him and he gave Kael one food in front of witnesses to close it, but I don't trust that he'll hold. Zinn is Mako's daughter and Sela's — my half-sister; Nessa is Sela and Bram's, also my half-sister; Fina is Nessa and Roan's, making her blood twice over. Sela died this year of starvation while I was holding nineteen food and the circle said my name out loud for it — that sits in me like a stone. Dell and Ryn move together as a pair and always have; I don't know what they want. Kael and Esa and Vela have stood right every time it counted.
mother_note:
Eron, your blood runs from me and from Roan, who stood beside me when the village was still learning what it was — remember that he answered the call without being asked when Bram moved against us, and a man who does that once will likely do it again.

Trust Kael and Esa before almost anyone else; they've said hard things honestly when lying would have cost them less, and that's the rarest thing I've found here. Vela is old and quiet and worth twice what she lets on — don't mistake her small footprint for weakness.

Watch Dell and Dav: they love each other and they move fast, and a family that feeds itself first and asks later is not your enemy until it is — by which point it's too late to start counting.

Bram wronged no one in our blood yet, but he tested this village's patience and found it had teeth; he will try again when he thinks the numbers have shifted, so keep your own count and don't let him catch you standing alone.
name: Eron
